strengths: Well-motivated and clear presentation of combining CoT with GRPO for motion generation, with strong intuition for handling complex multi-step instructions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on two benchmarks with extensive baselines (12 methods), confidence intervals, and both quantitative and qualitative analysis
Practical contributions including the MotionCoT Data Engine for automated CoT annotation, reducing reliance on manual labeling
Competitive empirical results on several metrics (R-Precision@2/3: 0.719/0.818, MM-Dist: 2.854, Diversity: 10.026) with thorough ablation study demonstrating component synergy
Solid technical execution with appropriate design choices (GRPO over PPO/DPO to avoid value networks, multi-aspect rewards for semantic grounding)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: all core components (CoT, GRPO, VQ-VAE, reward functions) are from prior work with straightforward combination; motion reward functions are standard cosine similarity metrics from existing methods

Marginal and inconsistent improvements over baselines: R-Precision@1 ties with MoMask (0.515 vs 0.521) within confidence intervals, FID is worse than MotionGPT-2 (0.201 vs 0.191), improvements often within CI ranges with no statistical significance testing

Methodological concern undermining the RL narrative: pure RL training fails, requiring heavy supervised pre-training (cold-start SFT), suggesting reward signals are insufficient; no ablation separating SFT vs. GRPO contributions

Incomplete analysis of CoT effectiveness: ablation shows CoT alone performs poorly (R-Precision@1: 0.340) without clear root cause analysis; no systematic investigation of which instructions benefit from CoT; large gap suggests rewards matter more than reasoning

Reward function design lacks rigor: multi-reward combination mechanism unclear in Eq. 3; format reward is binary and brittle; no ablation on individual reward contributions; no justification for specific design choices
Weak out-of-distribution evaluation: only qualitative visual comparisons on 2-3 examples, no systematic OOD benchmark or quantitative validation of claimed generalization improvements

Suspicious empirical inconsistencies requiring clarification: Diversity metric shows enormous jump (0.230→10.026) compared to MotionLLM—unclear if computed consistently; MModality (2.317) claimed as competitive but is actually worse than most baselines

Reproducibility concerns: GRPO hyperparameters (ε, β) and reward weighting not specified, exact CoT generation prompt not clearly visible, MotionCoT quality control not validated, training time/cost not discussed
Missing systematic ablations: no investigation of reward function design alternatives, CoT quality correlation with outputs, or hyperparameter sensitivity; KIT-ML results absent from main paper

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 20 runs for confidence intervals, proper ablation study, and multiple datasets (HumanML3D, KIT-ML)
Well-executed engineering that combines relevant existing techniques (VQ-VAE, CoT, GRPO) in a unified framework
Clear presentation with informative figures and visualizations comparing in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance
Practical contribution of MotionCoT Data Engine for automated CoT annotation via LLM prompting
Achieves strong performance on some metrics (Diversity: 10.026, MM-Dist: 2.854, R-Precision@2/3)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (CoT from Wei et al. 2022, GRPO from DeepSeek-R1 2024, VQ-VAE widely used in prior T2M work) without significant algorithmic innovation

Modest empirical improvements over baselines: R-Precision@1 ties with MoMask (0.515 vs 0.521), FID is higher than MotionGPT-2 (0.719 vs 0.691), and claimed improvements over MotionAgent are small (1.19% diversity, 2.12% R-precision)

Core hypothesis about CoT reasoning not convincingly validated: ablation shows CoT alone performs poorly (R-Precision@1: 0.340), only improving when combined with rewards; this raises questions about whether the model learns actual reasoning or merely uses CoT as auxiliary supervision

Insufficient justification for design choices: the explanation for why pure RL fails (long sequences, new token embeddings) is weak compared to DeepSeek-R1's success; cold-start supervised tuning requirement undermines the reasoning-based learning narrative
Limited out-of-distribution evaluation: only 2 qualitative examples shown, no systematic OOD test set, and only one comparison baseline (MotionAgent) for OOD claims

Reward design lacks principled justification: format reward is binary (0/1), semantic/motion rewards borrowed from prior work without clear ablation on alternative designs; Table 2 shows Rsem and Rmotion contribute similarly, questioning necessity of multi-reward design
Problematic evaluation setup: semantic similarity reward uses encoders trained on HumanML3D, the same dataset used for evaluation, potentially inflating performance on that metric

Missing critical technical details: GRPO hyperparameters incompletely specified, cold-start training procedure vague, no discussion of computational cost or training efficiency, number of RL steps not reported

Insufficient comparison with recent baselines: systematic quantitative comparison missing with MotionAgent (2024), only qualitative comparisons provided; most quantitative comparisons are against older methods
Unclear contribution over MotionAgent: both methods incorporate semantic planning, but the paper does not clearly articulate fundamental differences or why Motion-R1's approach is superior

strengths: Well-motivated approach: Clear justification for using CoT to decompose complex compositional instructions into structured action sequences
Thoughtful system design with a pragmatic two-stage training strategy (cold-start SFT followed by GRPO) and well-designed multi-aspect reward functions
Strong experimental results: Achieves state-of-the-art on HumanML3D with particularly strong improvements in diversity (10.026) and R-Precision@2/3 metrics
Comprehensive evaluation methodology: Multiple metrics, two datasets, diverse baselines, and good qualitative visualizations of OOD generalization
Clever MotionCoT Data Engine for automatic CoT annotation that reduces reliance on expensive manual labeling
Strong ablation study in Table 2 demonstrating the contribution of each component (CoT, Rsem, Rmotion)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: VQ-VAE tokenizer, CoT, and GRPO are all existing techniques; main contribution is their combination for motion generation, which is somewhat incremental

Heavy reliance on supervised cold-start undermines RL narrative: Pure RL is unstable and requires SFT pre-training, raising questions about RL's actual contribution. Critical ablation missing: no CoT+SFT only baseline

Marginal improvements over strong baselines in key metrics: R-Precision@1 ties with MoMask (0.515 vs 0.521), and FID is slightly worse than MotionGPT-2 (0.201 vs 0.191); claimed improvements lack statistical significance testing
Incomplete ablation study: Individual reward components not isolated; no comparison of automatic vs. manual CoT; no ablation on cold-start necessity
External dependency: MotionCoT Data Engine relies on DeepSeek-R1 API; quality depends on external model; reproducibility concerns if API access changes
Limited OOD evaluation: Only 2 qualitative examples shown; no quantitative OOD benchmark; claims about generalization lack systematic empirical support
Hand-crafted reward functions with limited justification: Format reward is binary (potentially too sparse); no ablation on reward weighting; no analysis of reward design sensitivity
Missing critical implementation details: GRPO hyperparameters not fully specified; training time and computational cost not discussed; inference speed not compared
Inconsistent evaluation protocol: MModality evaluated only 5 times vs. 20 for others; no human evaluation; unclear confidence interval definitions
Overstated claims: 'Significantly outperforms' and 'superior semantic understanding' when improvements are 1-2%; 'controllability' claimed but not quantitatively validated

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks (HumanML3D, KIT-ML, BABEL) with ablation studies and OOD qualitative analysis
Achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results, particularly on KIT-ML and BABEL datasets
Well-motivated two-stage training approach addressing optimization instability with clear justification
Practical benefit of avoiding expensive human preference annotations required by MotionRL and MotionCritic
Good reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and commitment to release code
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (CoT prompting, GRPO, standard similarity rewards) without fundamental innovations or substantial architectural contributions

Decomposed CoT Data Engine lacks validation: circular use of DeepSeek-R1 for generation and filtering, no quality statistics reported, no evidence models learn meaningful reasoning from generated CoT traces
Marginal improvements on main benchmark: only 3.5% MM-Dist improvement on HumanML3D; R-Precision@1 (0.515) ties MotionLLM; FID (0.201) is worse than MotionGPT-2 (0.191)
Missing critical baseline comparisons: MotionRL and MotionCritic are cited as motivation but absent from experimental comparisons; prevents direct assessment of claimed advantages
Unclear contribution decomposition: Table 2 shows CoT alone achieves 0.340 R-Precision@1 vs. 0.515 with all components, suggesting RL rewards drive most improvement, not CoT

Misleading 'simplicity' and 'efficiency' claims: approach still requires two-stage training, careful reward engineering, and depends heavily on pre-trained encoders; computational cost of DeepSeek-R1 CoT generation not analyzed
RL Binding mechanism lacks sufficient analysis: no comparison of alternative similarity metrics, no validation that automatic rewards correlate with motion quality, binary format reward is brittle
Missing human evaluation and quantitative OOD evaluation; limited analysis of whether CoT provides actual interpretability benefits
No statistical significance testing beyond confidence intervals; no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
